candidates.raw_excerpt: This action supplements a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published by the FAA in the Federal Register on June 17, 2025, which proposed to establish Class E domestic en route airspace (Class E6) within a designated landmass and within 12 miles from a designated shoreline associated with the state of Alaska to facilitate the vectoring of instrument flight rules (IFR) aircraft on direct routes where the current en route structure is insufficient or improper within the proposed airspace areas. As revised in this SNPRM, the FAA now proposes to establish five discrete areas of Class E domestic en route airspace over the state. Due to redundancy, the NPRM also proposed to remove two Class E6 airspace areas and modify 101 Class E airspace areas extending upward from at least 700 feet or more above the surface of the earth (Class E5) to remove any portion extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface. This SNPRM continues to propose these actions, but also now proposes to remove two Class E airspace areas extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface, revoke a duplicate Class E5 airspace legal description, and redefine airspace areas from a "Point of Origin" instead of using their respective airport reference points. Finally, both the NPRM and this SNPRM propose administrative amendments to the legal descriptions of 101 Class E5 airspace areas that would correct or update nomenclature as needed. This action would support IFR operations while enhancing the safety and management of aircraft operations within the National Airspace System (NAS).

candidates.title: Flight 14 waits on approval as a near-term manifest sketches Starship’s next steps
candidates.raw_excerpt: With Flight 14 being Starship’s first intended orbital mission, a near-term manifest is already pointing to the next two flights in close succession. Those dates look optimistic, and they may well slip, but they do confirm SpaceX is lining up a three-flight stretch from Flights 14 through 16: an orbital attempt from Starbase, a possible return to catching, and Starship’s expected East Coast debut. Booster 21 and Ship 41 rolled out earlier this week after months of pre-launch testing and preparations, then stacked at the pad for a wet dress rehearsal while SpaceX waited on approval. From the outside, that test appeared to go well. Both stages were fully loaded with propellant, there were no apparent holds at the optional T-minus 60-second hold point, and the count continued to just before engine ignition before the launch mount’s top-deck water deluge started and shut down a few seconds later. A full stack nearly a week before the planned launch had raised questions about timing, but SpaceX said teams were using the regulatory pause to get an extra rehearsal in. Earlier Starship versions rarely scrubbed close to launch; with Version 3, the first two flights have each seen a scrub of some kind. The extra pad time also put the launch mount back into use more than two months after the last flight. Approval could still arrive at any time, including over the weekend, so a Monday launch remains possible even without a license in hand tonight. candidates.title: Department of Justice Seizes Stablecoin Tether’s Bank Accounts
candidates.raw_excerpt: Ask any crypto bro for the digital equivalent of the gold-standard, and they’ll likely tell you about Tether — though a recent raid by the Department of Justice is throwing that characterization into question. Fresh reporting by the Financial Times revealed that the US Department of Justice has seized millions of dollars from a collection of bank accounts and crypto wallets linked to the finance tech company Tether Limited. The company is famously the issuer of the “stablecoin” Tether, a digital currency meant to maintain a relatively stable value based on the exchange rate of the US dollar. The company Tether was one of the subjects of a massive FBI probe, which discovered an unlicensed payment processing business, Capstone, that is now alleged to have placed hundreds of millions of dollars worth of illegal transfers. The convoluted case also involves Bitfinex, a cryptocurrency exchange owned by Tether’s parent company, iFinex. Basically, the payment processor Capstone is alleged to have misrepresented itself as an information technology firm in dealings with legitimate banks like Wells Fargo and JPMorgan Chase. In reality, according to the allegations, the company was engaged in a massive fraud scheme, in which people affiliated with Capstone misrepresented themselves as FBI agents in order to scam the elderly, whose money was then converted into crypto, Reuters reported . Based on the information available so far, the two crypto companies seem like unwitting bystanders rather than willing participants. Tether’s connection came by way of a relationship with a legal off-shore firm called EQIBank, which handled the flow of Tether’s money through Capstone. candidates.title: SpaceX Falcon 9 to launch classified mission for U.S. Space Force from West Coast
candidates.raw_excerpt: File photo of a Falcon 9 at Space Launch Complex 4-East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Image: SpaceX. SpaceX will conduct a launch for a secretive U.S. military satellite constellation before dawn on Saturday from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Liftoff of the USSF-385 mission atop a Falcon 9 is scheduled for 5:56 a.m. PDT (8:56 a.m. EDT / 1256 UTC) at the opening of a three-hour launch window. The rocket will take a southerly trajectory on departure from the pad at Space Launch Complex 4-East. Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 30 minutes prior to launch. The classified mission for the U.S. Space Force is thought to be the third in a series of flights to deploy satellites based on SpaceX’s Starshield, a version of a Starlink satellite intended for government use. The first satellites in this particular constellation were launched from Vandenberg on USSF-366 on Aug. 15 and USSF-153 on Sept. 10. Although the Space Force revealed no details about the missions, it cataloged 23 satellites in orbit following each launch. A similar classified mission, USSF-259, headed to a different orbit on Sept. 17 and appeared to carry 17 satellites. The first stage booster, B1100, is making its 10th flight and will land on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You’, around eight and a half minutes after launch. It will be the sixth and final Falcon 9 launch of the month from Vandenberg which has become the prime site for SpaceX as it shifts its focus at Cape Canaveral to Starship operations. Just one Falcon 9 flew from the company’s East Coast launch site in September.

candidates.title: Judges Warn That AI-Generated Lawslop Is Getting So Bad It’s Threatening Courts’ Ability to Function
candidates.raw_excerpt: AI doesn’t need superintelligence to bring America’s judicial system to its knees. The proliferation of AI-generated slop paraded as legitimate legal documentation is now so bad that Florida’s second-highest appellate is sounding the alarm. In an opinion issued last week, a panel of three judges for Florida’s Fourth District Court of Appeal excoriated an attorney whose filings carried the unmistakable imprint of — in the judges’ words — “AI slop.” That assessment, first reported by Reuters , came along with a notice that the offending attorney might be referred to the Florida bar for discipline, as well as a warning that the kinds of “frivolous, scattershot arguments” generated by AI are causing serious problems for courts’ ability to process cases. “Pro se litigants and lawyers can easily abuse AI to crank out extensive and confounding documents that cause delay, annoyance, and expense to the other side,” the opinion states. “Busy courts can drown in a flood of filings that are difficult to navigate. Abusive AI filing clogs dockets and undermines the administration of justice. Courts expect more from an attorney.” As for the attorney in question, the district court found family attorney Jaclyn Soroka had filed a motion which was “legally insufficient, frivolous, and untimely.” “An AI supercomputer would struggle to find meaning in some of the prose used in this case,” the judges roared. “Counsel’s arguments need to be comprehensible to human readers — the courts, opposing counsel, and the litigants.” In an interview with Law.com , Soroka denied using any AI to produce legal documents, explaining that “in my practice of law, in all matters, I do not use artificial intelligence to generate court filings.” More on AI: OpenAI Is Now Facing Over 50 Consumer Harm and Wrongful Death Lawsuits The post Judges Warn That AI-Generated Lawslop Is Getting So Bad It’s Threatening Courts’ Ability to Function appeared first on Futurism .
